section.title: The Call of Jeremiah
section.sectionRationale: This is the book's opening seam: before any oracle of judgment is spoken, the LORD establishes who is speaking and why he can be trusted. A priest's son from Anathoth is claimed before birth, commissioned despite his fear, and armed with two visions and a promise of protection, setting the terms for the long, hard ministry that follows.
section.thesis: The LORD forms, consecrates, and appoints Jeremiah as a prophet before his birth, and though Jeremiah feels only youth and fear, God's own presence and watchful word make him as unmovable as a fortified city against the kings, priests, and people who will oppose him.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the prophet introduced, priest and son of Judah's last kings; the call itself, formed and set apart before birth; two confirming visions, the almond branch and the boiling pot from the north; and the commission to stand, fortified against all opposition.

units.label: Introducing Jeremiah
units.note: a priest of Anathoth, spanning the last kings of Judah

verses.text: These are the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests in Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin.
The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah,
and through the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah, until the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah son of Josiah king of Judah, when the people of Jerusalem went into exile.
The word of the LORD came to me, saying:

“Before I {{yatsar|formed}} you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I {{qadash|set you apart}} 
and appointed you as a prophet to the nations.”
“Ah, Lord GOD,” I said, “I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!”

But the LORD told me: 
“Do not say, ‘I am only a child.’ For to everyone I send you, you must go, and all that I command you, you must speak.
Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you,” declares the LORD.

Then the LORD reached out His hand, touched my mouth, and said to me: 
“Behold, I have put My words in your mouth.

See, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, 
to build and plant.”

units.label: Two confirming visions
units.note: the almond branch and the boiling pot

verses.text:
And the word of the LORD came to me, asking, “Jeremiah, what do you see?” 
“I see a branch of an {{shaqed|almond}} tree,” I replied.
“You have observed correctly,” said the LORD, “for I am watching over My word to accomplish it.”

Again the word of the LORD came to me, asking, “What do you see?” 
“I see a boiling pot,” I replied, “and it is tilting toward us from the north.”
Then the LORD said to me, “Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land.

For I am about to summon all the clans and kingdoms of the north,” declares the LORD. 
“Their kings will come and set up their thrones at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem. They will attack all her surrounding walls and all the other cities of Judah.

I will pronounce My judgments against them for all their wickedness, because they have forsaken Me to burn incense to other gods 
and to worship the works of their own hands.
Get yourself ready. Stand up and tell them everything that I command you. Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them.

Now behold, this day I have made you like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you,” declares the LORD.

yatsar.gloss: To form or shape, the same verb used of the LORD forming man from dust in Genesis 2:7. Before Jeremiah drew a single breath, God was already the potter shaping this particular life for a particular purpose.

qadash.gloss: To set apart, consecrate, make holy for a specific use. Jeremiah's whole life, not merely his message, is marked out before birth as belonging to God's purpose, the same word used of priests and vessels devoted to the LORD's service.

shaqed.gloss: Almond, from a root meaning to watch or wake, since the almond tree is the first to bloom in late winter. The wordplay is deliberate, God shows Jeremiah an almond branch, shaqed, and answers, I am shoqed, watching, over My word to perform it.

basic.context: Jeremiah ministers to Judah across roughly four decades, from good King Josiah's reforms through the disastrous reigns that follow, right up to Jerusalem's fall and exile. Before any of the hard words to come, God tells Jeremiah plainly who he is and who has sent him: chosen before birth, appointed prophet to the nations, and promised protection despite fierce opposition from his own people.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical call narrative, not merely a literary device, and it explains why Jeremiah could keep speaking an unwelcome message for forty years without being silenced. The honest hard question is verse 5, before you were born I set you apart, which raises real questions about God's sovereign choice over a life before that person has done anything; the text itself does not resolve every philosophical question this raises, but it grounds Jeremiah's whole ministry in a purpose fixed before his own choices began.
basic.originalLanguages: God formed, yatsar, Jeremiah in the womb, the same verb used of forming Adam from the dust, and set him apart, qadash, the word used elsewhere of consecrating priests and holy things. The almond branch, shaqed, plays on the Hebrew word for watching, shoqed, God's pledge that He is watching over His word to bring it to pass.
basic.typology: Jeremiah, formed and appointed before birth, foreshadows Christ, who was likewise sent from the Father before the foundation of the world for a specific mission, and who, like Jeremiah, was a prophet rejected by His own people. Jeremiah's promised protection, a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, anticipates the greater and more costly faithfulness of Jesus, who was not delivered from death but through it.
basic.christ: Paul echoes this call in describing his own calling, set apart from my mother's womb, Galatians 1:15, showing that God's pattern of pre-birth calling extends into the New Testament and ultimately points to the Son, sent into the world before the world's foundation for the work of redemption, John 1:1 and Ephesians 1:4. Jeremiah's lifelong rejection by kings, priests, and people previews the greater rejection of the true Prophet, Jesus, who also stood alone and unmoved against every hostile power.
basic.god: God is sovereign over a life before it is lived, choosing and appointing Jeremiah for a purpose Jeremiah did not choose for himself. Yet God is also patient and near: He meets Jeremiah's fear not with rebuke but with reassurance, His own presence, His own words placed in the prophet's mouth, and His own promise, I am with you to deliver you.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 1:15 has Paul use nearly identical language of his own calling before birth. Exodus 4:10-12 shows Moses raising the same objection of inadequate speech, answered the same way. Isaiah 49:1-5 has the Servant of the LORD likewise called from the womb. Ezekiel 2:6 and 3:8-9 give a prophet the same command not to fear and the same promise of a face like flint.
basic.oneStory: This is the commissioning of the prophet whose forty years of ministry will carry Judah from the last days of faithful kingship through covenant unfaithfulness, siege, and exile, into the first clear promise of a new covenant. The pattern set here, chosen before birth, sent despite weakness, sustained only by God's presence, runs through Scripture to its fullest expression in Christ, the Prophet who was set apart before the world began and who was not overcome by those who opposed Him.

context.literary:
The chapter has a deliberate frame. Verses 1 to 3 are a superscription in the third person, the kind of heading that opens several prophetic books, and it ends by naming the exile at the other end of the ministry. Verses 4 to 19 then switch to the first person, and the book's first act is a short drama in which Jeremiah speaks only three times, in verses 6, 11 and 13, each time in a few words. Everything else is the LORD speaking.

The call follows a pattern familiar from Moses, Gideon and Isaiah: a divine address, an objection from the human side, a reassurance, a sign. What is unusual is the density of the verbs. Verse 5 stacks four, formed, known, set apart, appointed. Verse 10 piles six verbs onto one sentence, four of them about breaking and only two about building. Nowhere else in the book is the programme of the ministry stated so compactly, and the same six verbs return when the book looks back, in 18:7 to 10 and again in 31:28.

The two visions work as a pair of questions and answers, each opening with the same line, 'What do you see?' The first is good news about the word: it will be carried out. The second is the content of the word: trouble boils over from the north. Because the two images are chosen to sound alike in Hebrew and to look nothing alike, the passage teaches that the certainty of the word and the severity of the word are one thing seen from two sides.

Verses 17 to 19 close the movement by answering the fear of verse 6 and the opposition promised by verse 16. The promise of verse 8, 'I am with you to deliver you', returns almost word for word in verse 19, so the whole call is held together by a pledge at its beginning and end.
context.historical:
Anathoth lay a short walk north east of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, about three miles out. It was a priestly town. When Solomon banished the priest Abiathar from Jerusalem he sent him to his fields in Anathoth, 1 Kings 2:26, and some readers suspect Jeremiah's family descended from him, though the text never says so. The Hilkiah of verse 1 is probably not the high priest who found the Book of the Law in Josiah's reign, 2 Kings 22:8, and the book does not link them. What it does tell us is that Jeremiah grew up in a family trained to know the law and to keep the temple, and that he would one day be hunted by his own townsmen, Jeremiah 11:21.

The date matters. The thirteenth year of Josiah is conventionally set at 627 BC. Five years later, in Josiah's eighteenth year, the Book of the Law was found and the great reform began, 2 Kings 22 and 23. So Jeremiah was already speaking before the reform and spoke on through it, which helps explain the book's blend of hope and impatience: the king cleansed the temple, but the prophet kept asking whether hearts had followed. Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 trying to stop Pharaoh Neco, 2 Kings 23:29, and from there the kings named in verse 3 rise and fall quickly: Jehoiakim, who burned Jeremiah's scroll, Jeremiah 36, and Zedekiah, the last king.

Behind all of this was the shifting balance of power. Assyria was fading, Egypt was reaching north, and Babylon was rising. The 'clans and kingdoms of the north' of verse 15 were still unnamed when Jeremiah first heard them. By 605 Babylon had beaten Egypt at Carchemish, Jeremiah 46:2, and the pot he saw was on the boil.

A word on the text: the Greek Old Testament of Jeremiah is roughly one eighth shorter than the Hebrew and arranges the later chapters differently. Chapter 1 reads much the same in both.
context.canonical:
The call is built from earlier calls on purpose. Moses objected that he was slow of speech and was told that the LORD made the mouth and would teach him what to say, Exodus 4:10 to 12. Gideon pleaded his youth and was met with 'I will be with you', Judges 6:15 and 16. Isaiah's mouth was touched with a coal from the altar, Isaiah 6:6 and 7. Jeremiah's own mouth is touched in verse 9, and Deuteronomy 18:18, the promise of a prophet like Moses with the LORD's words in his mouth, hangs over the scene. Jeremiah is being presented to Israel as the Mosaic prophet for the hour of her crisis.

The Servant of Isaiah 49:1 speaks in nearly the same terms, called from the womb and named from his mother's body, with a mouth made like a sharp sword. Ezekiel, called in exile, is told to expect a forehead harder than flint, Ezekiel 3:8 and 9. Jeremiah then reaches back to this chapter at his lowest, when he cries out that the LORD has deceived him, 20:7 to 9, and curses the day of his birth, 20:14 to 18, a bitter answer to the God who knew him before it. The words promised in verse 9 become, when he tries to be silent, a fire in his bones.

In the New Testament Paul takes the language of verse 5 for his own apostleship, Galatians 1:15, and Luke tells of John the Baptist as one filled with the Spirit from the womb, Luke 1:15. Jesus meets the pattern of the unwelcome prophet at Nazareth, Luke 4:24, and Hebrews 1:1 and 2 gathers all the prophets, Jeremiah among them, into the final speech of the Son.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Whoever shaped the opening of this book wanted its first readers to settle one question before they read anything else: why listen to this man? The superscription ties Jeremiah to the temple, to the kings and to the exile, so that the words that follow cannot be waved off as a village priest's private opinion. The call then removes every ground except one. Jeremiah is not eloquent, not old, not courageous, and not eager. Whatever authority he has comes from the God who spoke first.

The book was also written for survivors. People who looked back from exile needed to know that the catastrophe was neither an accident of history nor evidence that the LORD had lost control. It had been announced, from the first day of the prophet's ministry, by a God who was watching over His word. Verse 12 is the hinge for that reading of history.

The call also tells the first hearers what kind of ministry to expect. Four verbs of demolition and two of construction mean that the final word is mercy, but the order is destruction first. A people who wanted only the planting would have to hear the uprooting. Anyone who later felt tempted to side with the prophets of peace, as many did, had been warned in verses 17 to 19 who would stand in the end.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how one man was commissioned; it does not tell readers to expect an audible voice, a vision of an almond branch, or a mouth touched by a hand. Nor does it promise that everyone who obeys God will be protected from harm. The fortified city of verse 18 sits beside the rest of the book, where Jeremiah is beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern, and watches his city burn. The promise of verse 19 is that his enemies will not overcome him, not that they will not fight him, and the book bears that out.

What does carry over is the pattern. God's purposes for a person come before the person's ability. A sense of inadequacy is not itself a reason to decline, but neither is it dismissed; the LORD answers it by giving His presence and His words rather than by flattering the prophet. Anyone who speaks for God, whether in a pulpit or at a kitchen table, is meant to speak what has been given and to keep speaking it when the audience is unwilling.

debates.question: What does 'I knew you' in verse 5 mean?

views.label: God's intimate, choosing knowledge
views.case: The verb is the ordinary Hebrew verb for know, but it often carries relationship and choice. In Amos 3:2 the LORD says to Israel, 'Only you have I known from all the families of the earth', and the sense is clearly chosen. The verbs around it, formed, set apart, appointed, are all acts of commissioning, so the knowing here is a personal claim, not bare information.

views.label: Foreknowledge of a life and its course
views.case: Some take the line closer to the New Testament's language of being known before the foundation of the world, Ephesians 1:4 and 1 Peter 1:20, as an affirmation that nothing about Jeremiah's life surprised God. On this reading the verse supports a robust doctrine of providence over a human life from conception.

views.label: A prophet's office only, not a general doctrine
views.case: Others stress that the verse speaks of Jeremiah's vocation, not of every person's eternal destiny. They caution against building a doctrine of election to salvation on it, since the passage never addresses who will be saved.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the text's purpose is pastoral: Jeremiah's task rests on a decision made before any act of his, and so no failure of his can cancel it. The verse invites trust, and it does not answer the whole question of predestination.

debates.question: Is the pot 'tilting' in verse 13, and who is the enemy from the north?

views.label: An unnamed, deliberately open threat
views.case: The text never names the northern power. Because the vision comes in Josiah's reign, some argue it describes a general northern menace that later events filled in, much as the lion and the storm of chapter 4 are images before they are armies.

views.label: Babylon from the start
views.case: Jeremiah later names the power: the LORD will summon 'all the families of the north' and 'My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon', 25:9. On this view the vision was always about the rising empire, even if the young prophet did not yet know its name.

views.label: Scythian raiders first, Babylon later
views.case: Some historians connect the early oracles with a northern nomad raid reported by Greek writers. Evidence for any such raid in Judah is slight, and most scholars now think the Babylonian reading fits the book better.

debates.bearing: Whichever identification is chosen, the theological claim of verse 15 is the same: the kings of the north are summoned by the LORD and set up their thrones in Jerusalem's gates only because He calls them there.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 5 uses four verbs and each one is a different kind of claim. Yatsar, formed, is the potter's verb, and it describes Jeremiah as a vessel shaped by hand; Jeremiah will watch a potter at work in chapter 18. Yada, know, is the verb of relationship and choice, as in Amos 3:2. Qadash, set apart, belongs to the vocabulary of the sanctuary: it is what is done to things and people made holy for the LORD's service. The last verb, the one the BSB renders 'appointed', is the common Hebrew verb for giving, natan. The same verb carries the next verses: in verse 9 the LORD says literally that He has given His words in Jeremiah's mouth, and in verse 18 He has given him as a fortified city. Everything Jeremiah is and says is a gift.

The title in verse 5, 'prophet to the nations', matters because later chapters take it literally: the book ends with a long run of oracles against foreign powers, and the cup of wrath goes round every nation in chapter 25.

The wordplay of verses 11 and 12 is the most famous in the book. The almond tree, shaqed, was the first to wake in late winter, and the LORD says that He is watching, shoqed, over His word. The BSB footnote preserves the pun: the Hebrew for watching sounds like the Hebrew for almond tree. The verb behind 'watching' is the verb of the wakeful guard, and Jeremiah 31:28 uses it again as the answer to chapter 1: the God who watched to uproot will watch to build and plant. The first vision is therefore a promise before it is a warning.

Verse 10 lists six verbs. Four describe pulling things down: to uproot, to tear down, to destroy, to overthrow. Two describe putting things up: to build and to plant. The imbalance is the point. The pulling down comes first and gets more words, but the last two verbs are the ones that last.

In verse 17 the BSB has 'Get yourself ready'. The Hebrew is the idiom of gathering up one's long robe to run or to fight, and the footnote gives it as 'Gird up your loins'. The same verse contains a sharp pun: 'Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them.' The verb is the same in both clauses. If Jeremiah is dismayed before them, God will leave him dismayed before them. Courage in the face of opposition is a command, and the one thing the LORD refuses to promise is a prophet who flinches and succeeds.

typology.type: The prophet with God's words in his mouth, Jeremiah 1:9
typology.fulfillment: Moses was promised a prophet like himself with the LORD's words in his mouth, Deuteronomy 18:18, and Jeremiah's touched mouth presents him as the Mosaic prophet for his hour. The pattern is completed in Jesus, who says that He speaks only what the Father has told Him, John 12:49 and 50, and who is called the Word, John 1:1 and 14. Jeremiah received the words as a gift to pass on; Christ is the Word. The type falls short because Jeremiah's words were fire and a hammer, 23:29, but they could not by themselves change the heart.

typology.type: A prophet set apart before birth, Jeremiah 1:5
typology.fulfillment: The pattern reaches Paul, Galatians 1:15, and Isaiah's Servant, Isaiah 49:1. In Christ the claim is stronger still: He was known before the foundation of the world, 1 Peter 1:20, and was with the Father before the world began, John 17:5. Jeremiah was chosen from the womb to serve the people of God; Jesus came from the Father to be their Redeemer. The correspondence is real but not exact, since Jeremiah was a sinner needing the same forgiveness he preached.

typology.type: The fortified city, iron pillar and bronze walls, Jeremiah 1:18
typology.fulfillment: A man made into a wall: a single faithful person standing in place of a crumbling city. Jesus stands the same way before rulers, priests and crowds, and holds firm to death, Isaiah 53:7 and John 18:37. Where Jeremiah's walls kept him through his enemies' attacks, Christ's endurance carried Him through death, and by His resurrection He is the foundation on which the church is built, Matthew 16:18. The type is limited: Jeremiah was delivered from the hands of men, but Jesus was handed over and raised, and His victory is shared with those who trust Him.

study.christ:
Chapter 1 does not mention a Messiah, but it sets up the shape of a ministry that the New Testament sees fulfilled in the Son. The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah and is put in his mouth; the author of Hebrews says that God, who spoke to the fathers through the prophets, has now spoken by His Son, Hebrews 1:1 and 2. The movement is from a mouth to a Person. Jeremiah's authority was borrowed, and the prophet had to say 'the word of the LORD came to me.' Jesus does not say that. He says, 'But I tell you', and in John's Gospel He is the Word Himself, John 1:1 and 14.

Jeremiah is also the prophet of a rejected message, and the evangelists notice the likeness. When Jesus is asked who people say He is, some answer Jeremiah, Matthew 16:14. The answer fits more than we may realise. Both wept over Jerusalem, both predicted the destruction of the temple, Jeremiah 7:14 and Mark 13:2, both were nearly killed for saying so, Jeremiah 26:8 and 9, and both were rejected in their hometowns, Jeremiah 11:21 and Luke 4:24. Jesus, then, comes in the line of the prophets and also at the end of it: He is the prophet who finally carries the people's sin, not only the people's warning.

The call can be read for its promise to build and plant, which is the last word of verse 10. Jeremiah himself prophesied the new covenant, 31:31 to 34, and Jesus says at the Last Supper that His blood is the new covenant, Luke 22:20. What was only a pair of verbs at the end of a list in chapter 1 becomes a Person. Care is needed here: the text of chapter 1 does not mean that Jeremiah is secretly about Christ in every verse, and it would be forcing the passage to find the cross in the almond branch. The link is the progression of a prophetic word that gathers force until it is fulfilled in One who is both the speaker and the message.

Finally, the fortified city is a promise for those who are in Christ. Paul quotes the same logic when he says that God's strength is made perfect in weakness, 2 Corinthians 12:9. The prophet who protests that he is only a child becomes the strong one, but only because the strength was never his.
study.god:
The God of this chapter acts before anyone asks. He forms, knows, sets apart and appoints; Jeremiah's only contribution is an objection. The first thing the passage teaches about God, then, is priority. Calling does not wait for readiness. This is not an arbitrary power, because verse 8 shows the intention behind it: He appoints in order to be with. 'I am with you to deliver you' is the line He says first and last.

The passage holds sovereignty and tenderness in one scene. A God who can make a boy a fortified city and who summons the kings of the north to the gates of Jerusalem is also the God who reaches out His hand and touches a frightened mouth. The two do not compete. The power in verse 15 is the same power that holds Jeremiah in verse 19, and a reader who sees only the judgment will miss that the God who judges is the God who protects His servant.

Verse 12 shows a God who is awake. He is not the absent deity His people accuse Him of being, and the book will later quote their complaint, that He seems like a stranger in the land, 14:8 and 9. The watching of verse 12 is the reply: He is watching over His word. A promise of watchfulness cuts both ways. His word of judgment will be performed with the same reliability as His word of comfort, and for that reason neither can be treated as an empty threat.

The passage also shows what God thinks of human weakness. He does not argue that Jeremiah is secretly strong. In verse 7 He refuses the claim of youth as a reason for refusal and gives no other reason for hope except Himself. Compare Exodus 4:11, where God reminds Moses that He made the mouth. In both places a reluctant servant is not taught to feel more able but to rely on the One who equips. Strength is a gift received in the act of obeying.

For worship this means that praise begins with His initiative. We speak of Him because He first spoke, we serve because He first set us apart, and we endure because He promised to be with us. The prophet's later honesty, the complaints and laments, is welcome in this relationship. The God who made Jeremiah a wall is not threatened by the prophet's cries from behind it.

crossReferences.note: Moses says he is slow of speech and tongue; the LORD answers that He made the mouth and will teach him what to say. Jeremiah's 'I do not know how to speak' meets the same reply, 'what I command you, you must speak', so the call places Jeremiah beside Moses.

Gideon pleads that he is the youngest in his father's house; the answer is simply 'I will be with you'. Like Jeremiah, he is told that the cure for smallness is God's presence, not a larger self-image.

Isaiah's lips are touched with a coal from the altar and his sin removed before he is sent. Jeremiah's mouth is touched too, but there is no confession of uncleanness; the contrast is of a prophet who is made ready by cleansing and one made ready by being given the words.

The Servant is called from the womb, named from his mother's body, and made a sharp sword and polished arrow, then discovers that he has laboured in vain. The parallel with Jeremiah is close, and Christians read the Servant as pointing past Jeremiah to Christ.

Ezekiel is told that his forehead will be harder than flint against a rebellious house. This is the same promise as Jeremiah's iron pillar and bronze wall: hardness given to the prophet, not to cause harm, but so he will not be broken.

The six verbs of 1:10 return here as a rule for how the LORD deals with nations: He announces uprooting and tearing down, and relents if the nation turns. The call turns out to be conditional in its warnings but fixed in its purpose to build.

The word for watching from the almond vision comes back: 'Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down... so I will watch over them to build and to plant.' The chapter 1 programme is answered here, and the same watchful God is behind both.

Jeremiah accuses the LORD of overpowering him, and says that the word became a fire shut up in his bones. This is the cost side of verse 9, where a word was put in his mouth and could not afterward be removed.

Jeremiah curses the day of his birth and wishes he had died in the womb. He reads the same womb as verse 5 of chapter 1 but with the blessing stripped out. The book leaves the tension unresolved, and the honesty is part of its comfort.

Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and called him by grace so that he would preach Christ among the Gentiles. He borrows Jeremiah's wording and his 'to the nations', and shows that the Old Testament pattern of calling carries into the apostles.

Jesus says that no prophet is accepted in his hometown. Jeremiah was threatened by the men of Anathoth, 11:21, and Jesus is nearly thrown off a cliff at Nazareth. The comment is the New Testament's own note that Jeremiah's experience is the usual prophet's experience, and that Jesus stood in it.
The many ways in which God spoke through the prophets are summed up in the Son. Jeremiah's mouth, touched by the LORD, is part of the many parts; the Son is the whole speech.

study.oneStory:
Before Jeremiah speaks a word, the Bible has already told a long story about words. God speaks and the world exists, Genesis 1. God speaks one prohibition and the human pair doubt it, Genesis 3:1. The word is given to Israel at Sinai and set in the heart of the covenant, and the people stop listening. By Jeremiah's day the nation has heard the word for eight hundred years, and chapter 1 presents the LORD's last, patient attempt to be heard: He puts the words into a human mouth and sends it to a people who are hostile. The call answers the question of how God will go on speaking to a people who will not hear.

It also looks back to the fall in another way. The prophets are the means by which God continues to walk toward His people when they hide. In Genesis 3:9 the LORD comes and asks, 'Where are you?' In Jeremiah 1:11 He asks, 'What do you see?' Both are questions from a God who will not leave humanity alone with its conclusions. Jeremiah's vision of the almond branch is a seed of the same hope that the LORD will make good what He has said.

The chapter then sets up what follows. The six verbs of verse 10 become the outline of the book: uprooting and tearing down in the first half, building and planting in the book of consolation, chapters 30 to 33, where the new covenant is promised. Verse 5's 'prophet to the nations' becomes the oracles against the nations in the closing chapters. The enemy from the north of verse 14 comes in earnest in chapters 4 to 6 and ends in the fall of Jerusalem in chapter 52.

Beyond the book, the pattern of the weak servant whom God makes strong runs to the cross. Christ is the faithful prophet who does not run, and by His death and resurrection He plants what Jeremiah could only promise. The last pages of the Bible show what was being built. The promised 'building and planting' is the city of Revelation 21 and the tree of life of 22:2, where the word of God is no longer an unwelcome message carried by a lone voice, but is simply the way the Lamb and His people live.

sermon.title: Chosen, Called, and Faithful
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly through Jeremiah 1:1-19, drawing out God's sovereign claim on a life before birth, the equipping of a fearful servant, and the confidence that comes from knowing God preserves those He appoints, exactly the movement this study traces.

quiz.q: What does God say about Jeremiah before he was even born?

options.text: That He formed him, knew him, set him apart, and appointed him a prophet to the nations.
options.note: Verse 5 grounds Jeremiah's entire ministry in a purpose fixed before his birth.

options.text: That he would become a priest like his father Hilkiah.
options.note: Jeremiah was from a priestly family, but God's specific word appoints him a prophet, not a priest.

options.text: That he would live a long and comfortable life.
options.note: The chapter promises deliverance amid conflict, not comfort or ease.

options.text: Nothing; the call came only as an adult.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly speaks of God's purpose before Jeremiah was formed in the womb.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah initially respond to his call?

options.text: With an objection that he does not know how to speak and is only a child.
options.note: Verse 6 records Jeremiah's honest sense of inadequacy, met by God's reassurance rather than rebuke.

options.text: With immediate, confident acceptance and no hesitation.
options.note: Jeremiah does ultimately serve faithfully, but his first response is hesitant, not confident.

options.text: By refusing outright and fleeing the country.
options.note: Jeremiah raises an objection but does not refuse or flee; he goes on to serve for decades.

options.text: By demanding a sign before he would believe God.
options.note: His objection is about his own inadequacy, not a demand for proof.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the almond branch vision in verses 11-12?

options.text: It plays on the Hebrew words for almond and watching, confirming God is watching over His word to fulfill it.
options.note: Shaqed, almond, and shoqed, watching, form a deliberate wordplay assuring Jeremiah that God's word will not fail.

options.text: It predicts a literal famine caused by a lack of almonds.
options.note: The vision is about God's watchfulness over His word, not agricultural conditions.

options.text: It is simply a random object with no theological meaning.
options.note: The vision carries clear theological weight through its wordplay.

options.text: It symbolizes the sweetness of the message Jeremiah will preach.
options.note: Jeremiah's message will be largely one of judgment, not sweetness; the vision's point is God's watchfulness.

quiz.q: What promise does God give Jeremiah to sustain him against opposition?

options.text: That He will make Jeremiah like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, and be with him to deliver him.
options.note: Verses 18-19 promise not the absence of conflict but God's presence and preservation within it.

options.text: That no one in Judah will ever oppose him.
options.note: The text explicitly says kings, officials, priests, and people will fight against him.

options.text: That his ministry will be short and painless.
options.note: Jeremiah's ministry spans roughly forty years and is marked by suffering, not ease.

options.text: That he will be given political power over Judah's kings.
options.note: The image of nations and kingdoms in verse 10 is about his prophetic word's authority, not political rule.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah's call anticipate the New Testament?

options.text: Paul describes his own apostolic calling in nearly identical language, set apart from his mother's womb.
options.note: Galatians 1:15 deliberately echoes Jeremiah 1:5, showing the same pattern of pre-birth calling continuing into apostolic ministry.

options.text: It has no connection to anything in the New Testament.
options.note: Paul's language in Galatians 1:15 directly echoes this passage.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Christ's birth.
options.note: The passage speaks of calling and purpose, not chronological prediction.

options.text: It shows that all New Testament believers receive audible calls with visions.
options.note: The pattern of purposeful calling extends to Paul, but Scripture does not generalize identical audible calls and visions to all believers.

questions: God says He knew and set Jeremiah apart before he was born. How does knowing your life has purpose, even before you could choose anything, change how you face what God calls you to now?
Jeremiah's honest objection, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a child, was met with reassurance rather than rejection. Where are you hiding from a calling because you feel unqualified?
God's answer to Jeremiah's fear was not a change of circumstance but a promise of presence, I am with you to deliver you. Where do you need that same promise more than a change in your situation?

The almond branch reminded Jeremiah that God is watching over His word to perform it. What promise of God do you need to trust is being watched over and brought to pass, even though you cannot yet see it?
God made Jeremiah a fortified city against real opposition, not an easy road. Where might God be calling you to stand firm rather than promising you an easier path?

translationNotes.note: Set apart translates a Hebrew verb, qadash, elsewhere rendered consecrated or sanctified; some English versions render it consecrated, but the underlying idea, set apart wholly for God's use, is the same.
The wordplay between almond, shaqed, and watching, shoqed, is audible in Hebrew but invisible in English translation; the BSB footnote or study notes typically flag this pun.

Fortified city, iron pillar, and bronze walls are three distinct images of unbreakable strength; some translations render the second as pillar of iron, but the sense of impregnable defense is the same across versions.
